name: Seven Sisters Waterfall
image_query: Seven Sisters Waterfall Sikkim North Sikkim Highway
tagline: A roadside cascade in the Kabi forest on the way to Phodong
meta_description: Seven Sisters Waterfall on the North Sikkim Highway near Kabi Lungchok: a free roadside stop between Gangtok and Phodong. Best months, safety, costs and tips.
summary: The Seven Sisters Waterfall is a roadside cascade on the North Sikkim Highway in the forest near Kabi Lungchok, roughly 25 to 30 km north of Gangtok and before Phodong. Wikipedia names it as one of the waterfalls in the Kabi area. It is a free 10 to 20 minute stop, needs no permit for Indian visitors and flows strongest in the monsoon.
intro: The Seven Sisters Waterfall falls beside the North Sikkim Highway in the forest around Kabi Lungchok, about 25 to 30 km north of Gangtok by our reckoning, between the Kabi memorial and Phodong. Wikipedia's article on Kabi Lungchok, citing ENVIS Sikkim, mentions a number of waterfalls in the area, one of which is known as the Seven Sister waterfalls. We have not found a published height or flow figure, so we give none.

You see it from the road, usually from a pull-off where drivers stop for photographs and tea. The water comes down in several streams over dark rock, which is presumably how it earned its name, and the spray cools the air. Flow is heaviest during the June to September monsoon and thinner in the dry months from November to March.

It is a stop and not a destination, and it fits naturally in a day loop with Kabi Lungchok and Phodong. It is outside the protected areas, so Indian visitors need no protected area permit. Roadside stops on this highway are exposed to traffic and slides, so keep the visit short and check current status before you travel.

story.title: A name on a busy road
story.text: We have not found a documented history for the name Seven Sisters Waterfall in Sikkim, and we do not repeat any story about it that lacks a source. What a written source does tell us is where it sits. Wikipedia's article on Kabi Lungchok says that the historical site is in dense forest on the North Sikkim Highway, in an area rich in streams, waterfalls and cultural monuments, and that one of the waterfalls there is known as the Seven Sister waterfalls. The article, citing the ENVIS Centre for Sikkim, lists the forest as subtropical mixed broad-leaved hill forest, with trees such as Nepal alder (Alnus nepalensis), Castanopsis and Toona ciliata. A waterfall in such a forest is fed by small mountain streams, so its volume follows the rains. That is the honest, checkable part, and we leave the rest to locals, who may tell you more. Ask your driver what the name means to him.

little_known.fact: Wikipedia's Kabi Lungchok article says there are a number of waterfalls in the Kabi area, and that one of them is known as the Seven Sister waterfalls.
The surrounding forest is classified as subtropical mixed broad-leaved hill forest, with Nepal alder, Castanopsis, Macaranga and Toona ciliata among the trees recorded.
The Kabi area is recorded as home to birds such as the crested serpent eagle, rufous-necked hornbill and Ward's trogon, so quiet mornings near the falls are worth a look and listen.

facts: October to May for roads; strongest flow June to September
Not needed for Indian visitors; foreigners need the Sikkim restricted area permit

highlights.title: A roadside cascade
highlights.text: The water falls in several streams over dark rock beside the highway, within sight of the road. Stop at the pull-off, step out for a few minutes and keep clear of the road edge and the spray, because the rock is slippery.

highlights.title: Monsoon force
highlights.text: From June to September the falls are at their fullest, though slides and spray can make the road hazardous. In the dry months from November to March they are thinner but easier to visit. Check current status before you travel.

highlights.title: Tea and a photo
highlights.text: Drivers on the North Sikkim route often stop here for photographs, and small stalls sometimes serve tea. This is a good place to stretch your legs after the climb out of Gangtok.

highlights.title: Forest all around
highlights.text: The falls sit in the subtropical broad-leaved forest that surrounds Kabi Lungchok. Listen for birds in the early morning and look for ferns and moss on the rock faces. Do not pick plants or disturb wildlife.

highlights.title: Part of a loop
highlights.text: The falls fit between Kabi Lungchok and Phodong, so a single car can cover Tashi View Point, Kabi, the falls, Phodong and Labrang in a day from Gangtok.

how_to_reach.text: Shared jeeps to Mangan pass the falls, and the driver may stop briefly if you ask beforehand, though this is not guaranteed. Fares to Mangan are roughly ₹300 to 450 a seat, indicative. There is no separate service to the falls.

A reserved small car from Gangtok takes about an hour to reach the falls, depending on traffic and road work. A day loop with Kabi Lungchok and Phodong is indicatively ₹3,000 to 4,500. The highway can close after monsoon slides.
Go to Gangtok first, 4.5 to 5 hours on NH10 from either, longer via Kalimpong or Algarah when NH10 is closed by slides. Visit the falls on a day trip or on your way north.

costs: Shared jeep Gangtok to Mangan (passes the falls)
Free, as far as we know
where_to_stay: There are no tourist stays at the falls and we do not plan nights here. Most visitors see them on a day trip or on the way north from Gangtok. For a night near Phodong, ask us about small lodges and homestays, whose availability varies. Mangan, further north, has simple hotels, and Gangtok has the widest choice, with budget rooms around ₹1,500 to 3,000 a night.
tips: Keep the stop to 10 or 20 minutes and park well off the carriageway.
Stay back from the water and wet rock, which is slippery, especially in the monsoon.
Do not cross the road with a camera in hand, as drivers on blind bends cannot see you in time.
Carry a rain jacket and a refillable bottle, and take your litter with you.
Ask your driver about slides ahead before the monsoon drive, and check current status before you travel.

experiences.title: A short stop at the Seven Sisters Waterfall
experiences.summary: Stop at the pull-off beside the falls, watch the water in several streams over dark rock and take a few photographs. A quick, free break on the drive between Gangtok and Phodong, best done with an eye on the road.
body: The falls are visible from the highway, and drivers know the pull-off. Step out, look at the water falling in several streams and feel the cool spray if the flow is strong. The sound carries up the road, and the rock around it is dark and wet.

Keep the visit short. Park off the carriageway, watch for traffic on blind bends and do not climb the wet rock to get closer. The edge of the road is narrow, and vehicles on the North Sikkim Highway do not slow for photographers.

Fit it into a day loop with Kabi Lungchok and Phodong rather than making a special trip. In the monsoon the flow is strongest, but slides can close the road, so check current status before you travel and ask your driver about conditions.

faqs.q: How long should we stop at the Seven Sisters Waterfall?
faqs.a: Ten to twenty minutes is enough for a look, photographs and a cup of tea if a stall is open. Longer stops add little, and the road edge is narrow. Keep the stop short on busy days and when the road is wet.

faqs.q: Is it safe to go close to the water?
faqs.a: We advise against it. The rocks are wet and slippery, the flow rises quickly after rain, and the road edge is exposed to traffic. Watch from the pull-off or a safe spot your driver chooses, and keep children close at all times.

faqs.q: Is there an entry fee?
faqs.a: As far as we know, no. It is a roadside waterfall with a pull-off and sometimes a tea stall. Arrangements can change, so check current status before you travel and ask your driver for the best stopping point.

experiences.title: Waterfall in the monsoon and in the dry months
experiences.best_time: June to September for flow; November to March for easy roads
experiences.summary: Compare the same falls across the year: strongest and loudest in the June to September monsoon, thinner and clearer in winter. We explain what to expect, and why the best waterfall month is not always the best travel month.
body: Waterfalls in Sikkim's hill forests are fed by rain and small streams, so the flow follows the season. From June to September the Seven Sisters Waterfall is at its fullest, with a loud, white flow and a lot of spray. Wikipedia's article on Kabi Lungchok records many streams and waterfalls in the area, one of them being this one.

The price of the monsoon show is the road. Slides can close the North Sikkim Highway and NH10 for hours or days, and the pull-off can be muddy and unsafe. If you are visiting in these months, keep your plans flexible, start early and ask your driver about the road before leaving Gangtok.

From November to March the falls are thinner, but the roads are more reliable and the air is clearer. Autumn, in October and November, gives a fair flow after the rains and good views across the valley. Check current status before you travel, in any season.

faqs.q: When are the falls at their best?
faqs.a: Flow is strongest in the June to September monsoon, but road conditions are at their worst, with frequent slides. October and November give a good flow after the rains and clearer weather. Winter flow is thinner. Check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: Is the road open in the monsoon?
faqs.a: Usually, but slides can close the North Sikkim Highway and NH10 for hours or days, and the closures are unpredictable. If you travel in the monsoon, keep a flexible plan and allow an extra day. Check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: Do the falls dry up in winter?
faqs.a: We have no record of them stopping, but the flow is reduced in the dry months from November to March, and spray is lighter. We do not have a measured figure, so ask your driver or check current status before you travel.

experiences.title: Birdsong by the falls
experiences.best_time: Early morning, March to May and October to November
experiences.summary: Listen and look for birds in the forest around the falls before the traffic builds up. The Kabi area is recorded as home to species such as the crested serpent eagle and Ward's trogon, though sightings are never guaranteed.
body: Wikipedia's article on Kabi Lungchok, citing ENVIS Sikkim, lists birds recorded in the area, including the pariah kite, crested serpent eagle, rufous-necked hornbill, chestnut-breasted partridge, black-breasted parrotbill, grey-crowned prinia and Ward's trogon. These records cover the wider Kabi area and are not specific to the falls, and we promise no sightings.

Come early, in the first hour after sunrise, when traffic is thin. Stand at the pull-off, stay quiet and listen before you look. The sound of the water covers some calls, so move a short distance along the road for a better chance. Binoculars help.

Stay on the verge, and keep clear of the road edge and the wet rock. Do not play recorded calls, and do not leave the track to follow a bird. In the monsoon, leeches and slides make this a poor choice. Check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: What birds are recorded near the falls?
faqs.a: Wikipedia lists the crested serpent eagle, rufous-necked hornbill, Ward's trogon, black-breasted parrotbill and others for the Kabi area, citing ENVIS Sikkim. These records are not specific to the falls. Sightings depend on luck, season and patience, so we never promise any.

faqs.q: What is the best time of day for birds?
faqs.a: The first hour after sunrise, when the forest is quiet and traffic is light. Late afternoon can also be good. Midday is quiet for birds, and the sound of the falls hides many calls. Check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: Do we need a guide?
faqs.a: Not for a short roadside stop, but a local guide who knows the calls improves your chances a lot. Ask us in advance if you want one, and mention the season. Do not play recorded calls to attract birds, and keep to the road verge.

experiences.title: A tea and picnic break on the road north
experiences.summary: Use the falls as a natural pause between Gangtok and Phodong: a cup of tea, some snacks and a stretch before the road climbs again. A modest, low-cost break with a good sound and a cooler breeze.
body: Small stalls near roadside waterfalls in Sikkim usually serve tea, instant noodles and biscuits, though we cannot promise that one will be open when you pass. Ask your driver. If no stall is open, carry a flask and snacks from Gangtok, and use the pull-off for a short rest.

Keep it simple and clean. Take your litter with you, use the bin if there is one and do not leave plastic in the stream. Carry a refillable bottle. Prices are low, roughly ₹20 to 50 for tea and ₹50 to 150 for a snack, indicative, and you should pay in small notes.

For a proper meal, Phodong's bazaar, about 10 to 15 km further north, has simple eating places, and Mangan has more. Leave Gangtok by 8:30 am so lunch falls at Phodong. Check current status before you travel, and watch the time if you are heading to the Toong check post.

faqs.q: Can we have lunch at the falls?
faqs.a: Not reliably. Small stalls may serve tea and snacks, but a proper meal is better at Phodong or Mangan. Carry water and snacks if you are travelling with children or older people. Check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: How much does tea cost at a roadside stall?
faqs.a: Roughly ₹20 to 50 for tea and ₹50 to 150 for noodles or snacks, indicative. Prices vary by stall and season. Carry small notes, and ask the price before ordering.

faqs.q: Where can we use a toilet?
faqs.a: Facilities at the pull-off are limited or absent, so plan for a toilet stop at Gangtok before you leave, at Phodong or at a stall that offers one. Check current status before you travel and ask your driver.

faqs.q: Where is the Seven Sisters Waterfall?
faqs.a: It is beside the North Sikkim Highway in the forest near Kabi Lungchok, roughly 25 to 30 km north of Gangtok by our estimate, before Phodong. Your driver will know the pull-off. We give the distance as approximate, and it takes about an hour from Gangtok.

faqs.q: How tall is the Seven Sisters Waterfall?
faqs.a: We have not found a published height and do not quote one. It is a roadside cascade that falls in several streams over dark rock and is seen from the road. Flow varies strongly with season, and is greatest in the monsoon.

faqs.q: Do I need a permit for the waterfall?
faqs.a: No protected area permit is needed for Indian visitors, since the falls are outside the protected areas. Foreign nationals need the online Sikkim restricted area permit to be in the state. Rules change, so check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: Is there an entry fee?
faqs.a: As far as we know, no. It is a roadside waterfall with a pull-off. Fees can change, so check current status before you travel and ask your driver or hotel in Gangtok.

faqs.q: What is the best time to see the waterfall?
faqs.a: Flow is strongest from June to September, but the monsoon is also when slides close the road. October and November offer a good flow and clearer weather. Winter flow is thinner. Check current status before you travel, in any season.

faqs.q: How long should we stop?
faqs.a: Ten to twenty minutes is enough for a look, a few photographs and a cup of tea. The road edge is narrow, so longer stops add little. A combined stop with Kabi Lungchok adds about 30 minutes.

faqs.q: Is it safe to swim or bathe at the waterfall?
faqs.a: No. We advise against going into the water, since rocks are wet and slippery, flow can rise quickly after rain and the site is beside a working road. Watch from the pull-off and keep children close.

faqs.q: Why is it called Seven Sisters?
faqs.a: We have not found a documented origin for the name, and we do not repeat unsourced stories. Wikipedia's Kabi Lungchok article says only that one of the waterfalls in the area is known as the Seven Sister waterfalls. A local driver may tell you more.

faqs.q: Is the waterfall worth the stop?
faqs.a: Yes, as a short stop on the way to Phodong. It is free, quick and easy, and the sound and spray are a pleasant break from the road. It is not worth a special trip, but it pairs well with Kabi Lungchok.
